sections.report:
The checklist walk, for the record (it is not part of the report):

Whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no.
- Purpose in one sentence: yes.
- Image and headline make one idea: no. Every card picture is a flat colour field with a pale circle, which is a placeholder, not a garden.
- Every element does a job: yes, except the placeholder circles, which are filed under the line above.
- Type, colour and shape share one mood: yes.
- Copy finished: yes.
- Repeated elements look the same: no. The Rose arch title and caption sit higher than the other five.
- Colour and shape carry the mood: yes.
- Headings name their content: yes.

Bash was refused, so the crop and entries scripts couldn't run. The image is one screen (about 1280×800), so I judged from the whole image, and the deep read used the checklist wording rather than the full entries.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No.
   - **Where:** All six card pictures. The top row runs from x 60 to 1220 at y 78 to 278, and the bottom row from y 392 to 592. Each picture is one flat colour (brick red, green, blue, brown, mustard, purple) with a pale circle cut off at its bottom edge.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The page says "Garden show gallery", but nothing in it shows a garden. The viewer can't see the rose arch, the herb bed or the pond. Only the titles say what each card is. A gallery whose pictures carry no content fails at the one thing a gallery is for. The pictures and the captions don't make one idea together, because the pictures hold no idea at all.
   - **Why:** These look like image placeholders or pictures that didn't load. If real photos replace them when the page is live, this is fine; check that in a live browser. As shown, it's a defect.
   - **Fix:** Put a real photograph of each garden in each frame, cropped so the subject fills the frame. Captions such as "Climbing roses over the east gate" should then add something the photo can't show.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.
2. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** No.
   - **Where:** Under the first card. The "Rose arch" title sits about y 298 and its caption about y 320. The other two top cards have the title at about y 300 and the caption at about y 324. So the first card's text block starts about 2 px higher and has about 2 px less space between title and caption.
   - **What the viewer meets:** Side by side, the left caption line sits visibly higher than its neighbours. The row looks slightly off, as if that card was styled on its own.
   - **Why:** This is common sense: repeated cards should follow one layout rule. It's a small slip, but it shows on a page made of six identical units.
   - **Fix:** Give all six cards the same title and caption spacing.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, minor.

**What's working.**
- Every card title names exactly what it shows ("Herb bed", "Pond edge"), and every caption adds a concrete fact ("Tomatoes in late July."). A visitor learns what each spot is without guessing.
- The six cards share one plain sans, one title/caption pattern and one card shape. Apart from the slip above, the page reads as one designed whole, not a collage.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the flat colour-and-circle frames are placeholders the live page replaces with photographs. Check in a browser after the images load.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; repeated elements look the same everywhere).

sections.report:
Walk (working notes):
- One element stands clearly above the rest: **no**. Six equal colour tiles fill the page. The page title "Garden show gallery" (60,38) is about 20 px bold, which looks smaller than the card titles. Nothing leads.
- Text levels distinct, no two sizes almost the same: **no**. The page title (~20 px) and the card titles (~22 px) are nearly the same size, and the order is inverted.
- Headings differ in weight, form or colour: **yes**. Card titles are bold and near-black; descriptions are regular and grey.

Bash is denied in this session, so I couldn't run the entries script or the crop script. I judged from the full image (1280×800, about one screen, so no crops were needed) and from the checklist's entry titles.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No.
   - **Where:** The whole grid, six tiles of 377×200 px at x 60–1220, y 78–592, plus the page title at about (60, 38–58).
   - **What the viewer meets:** All six tiles have the same size, the same strong saturated fill and the same pale centred circle. The eye has no starting point and moves across six equal blocks of colour. The only element meant to frame the page, "Garden show gallery", is the smallest heading on it and gets lost above the bright red tile.
   - **Why:** An equal grid is a fair convention for a gallery, where items are peers (`layout.md` "One element dominates" allows for this when the items really are equal). But here nothing at all leads: not a featured item, and not the title either. The saturated fills (red, yellow, purple) all have equal pull, so no one of them wins by contrast.
   - **Fix:** Make the page title clearly the top level, with a big step up in size, so the page announces itself before the grid starts. If one exhibit matters more (a featured garden or the current show), let it take a larger tile.
   - **Kind:** Defect for the title. Taste for any featured tile. **Weight:** major.
2. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No.
   - **Where:** The page title "Garden show gallery" (about 20 px bold, y ≈ 48) against the card titles "Rose arch", "Herb bed" and the rest (about 22 px bold, y ≈ 298–614).
   - **What the viewer meets:** The two sizes are only a couple of pixels apart and have the same weight and colour, so they read as one level. The card titles even look slightly larger, which turns the order upside down: the page heading looks like a seventh caption that has lost its card.
   - **Why:** Sizes only a few points apart read as mistakes, not as levels (Bringhurst, the type scale; `typography.md` "Weak contrast is worse than none", "Sizes come from a scale").
   - **Fix:** Pull the page title well clear of the card titles, for example about 1.5–2× their size. Or, if the title must stay small, drop the card titles a step so the gap is obvious. Measure both in the browser to confirm the inversion.
   - **Kind:** Defect. **Weight:** major. It is minor on its own but becomes major together with finding 1, because it is the reason nothing leads.

**What's working.**
- **Card titles against descriptions:** Within each card, the bold near-black title over the regular grey description (for example "Pond edge" / "Reeds and water lilies.") is a clean two-level pair. It uses weight and colour, not just size, so the name is read before the detail. Keep it.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Picture content:** The tiles look like placeholders (a flat fill with a pale circle). If real photographs replace them, the balance of pull across the grid will change and finding 1 should be checked again with the real images.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 1 yes, 2 no (one element dominates; text levels distinct), 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, with no near-misses? / Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** In row 1, the "Rose arch" caption looks about 2 px higher than "Herb bed" and "Pond edge": the title sits near y≈298 against ≈300. Its description, "Climbing roses over the east gate.", looks about 4 px higher, near y≈320 against ≈324. That also makes the space between title and description tighter in that card than in the other five. In row 2, all three captions share baselines (titles ≈614, descriptions ≈638), so only this one card is off. A viewer scanning across row 1 sees the first caption sitting slightly high. It doesn't look like a choice; it looks like a mistake, and it makes an otherwise tidy grid look unfinished (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a placement that is almost aligned reads as an error; Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*: elements meant to match share one spacing). The likely cause is different spacing or line-height on that one card. Fix it by giving all six cards the same space between image and title and between title and description, so captions in each row share baselines. The offsets are judged by eye from a still, so measure the caption tops in the live page to confirm. Mark: defect. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **The grid.** Three equal columns (about x 60–437, 451–829, 843–1220) with one even gutter of about 14 px repeat in both rows. The heading and both rows share the 60 px left edge, so the page reads as one system.
- **Spacing that shows the groups.** Each image sits about 20 px from its own caption, and the rows are about 60 px apart, so every caption clearly belongs to the picture above it and never to the row below.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (exact alignment with no near-misses; baselines across columns).

I zoomed in on the caption text to check its size and contrast. Next I'll go through the Text checklist and then write the report.

**Walk (Text, working notes):** Body text large enough: yes (the captions, about 14 px, are the body). Captions large enough: yes. Plain upright face: yes (one sans-serif). One family: yes. Small-text weight: yes. Contrast: yes (dark grey captions on white look well above 4.5:1). Text over image: yes (none). Line length: yes (single short lines). Leading: yes. Multi-line heading: yes (none). Flush left: yes. Justified: yes (none). Rag: yes. Widows: yes. Heading breaks: yes. Paragraph marks: yes. Left edge crisp: yes. Long text chunked: yes. Mixed case: yes. Emphasis: yes. Display spacing: yes. Kerning: yes. Tracking: yes. Caps letterspaced: yes (none). Ligatures: yes (no fi/fl in large type). Real cuts: yes. Quotes/dashes: yes (none). Tabular figures: yes (none). Real type: yes. Nothing clipped: yes.

Every line is yes, so step 5 has no entries to open.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

I noticed one thing that no Text line covers, so the director can file it under Arrangement. The first card's text sits higher than in the other cards. "Rose arch" is at about y≈298 and its caption at about y≈320. In the other two cards of that row, the title is at about y≈300 and the caption at about y≈324. So the gap between the first title and its caption is about 2 px tighter, and the first row's baselines don't line up across the three columns. It's a small defect in consistency.

**What's working.**
- **Type scale:** The page uses three sizes with plain jobs: the page title (about 20 px bold), the card titles (about 20 px bold), and the captions (about 14 px regular grey). Weight and colour tell the levels apart rather than near-duplicate sizes, so each card reads as a title with a note under it (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger).
- **Captions:** Each one is a single short, specific line ("Climbing roses over the east gate."). They're dark grey on white, readable, and need no line-length or rag handling.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece use a small palette, about one neutral range and one or two hues besides the status colors?** No.
   - **Where:** the six tiles each have their own unrelated saturated hue: brick red (60,78), sage green (451,78), steel blue (843,78), olive-brown (60,392), mustard gold (451,392) and purple (843,392). Each sits on the white and gray-text neutral.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the hues share no system, so the grid reads as six swatches from a default chart palette, not as one show's gallery. The colors carry no information. Color doesn't group the tiles, rank them, or tie them to the garden, so all that strength is spent for nothing.
   - **Why:** Albers and Itten (art-direction "Limited, purposeful palette": "each color has a job; many unrelated saturated hues are a fault"); Refactoring UI, "Define your shades".
   - **Fix:** if these flat tiles are what ships, draw them from one family, such as muted garden tints of one or two related hues, so each color has a job. If they only stand in for photographs, the finding goes away once real photos are in, because the rule counts hues outside photos.
   - **Kind:** convention. **Weight:** major if the tiles ship as they are, minor if they are placeholders.
2. **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** No.
   - **Where:** the six 377×200 px tiles cover about 450,000 px, roughly 44% of the 1280×800 canvas. All six are at about the same full strength. The pale circles inside are tints of the same hue and add no rest.
   - **What the viewer sees:** saturated color fills almost half the page and no tile is stronger than another, so nothing works as an accent. The eye gets a field of loud blocks with nowhere to settle. The dark captions under the tiles look weak next to them, even though they are the only thing that tells you what each tile is.
   - **Why:** Itten, contrast of saturation; Refactoring UI ("Saturation hierarchy": large areas of fully saturated color tire the eye and weaken emphasis).
   - **Fix:** use a muted or tinted version of each hue for the tile fields and keep full strength for small details, or let real photos carry the color.
   - **Kind:** convention. **Weight:** major if the tiles ship as they are, minor if they are placeholders.
3. **Do warm colors sit on what should come forward and cool ones on what should recede?** No.
   - **Where:** the brick red "Rose arch" tile (top left) and the mustard "Glasshouse" tile (bottom middle) jump forward. The blue "Pond edge" and purple "Orchard path" tiles fall back.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the six entries are peers, but temperature alone makes Rose arch and Glasshouse look featured. The eye lands on them first for no reason the content gives. The gold tile is also much lighter in value than the rest, which makes the uneven weight worse.
   - **Why:** Itten, warm–cool contrast.
   - **Fix:** if no entry is featured, even out temperature and value across the tiles. If one is featured, give it the warm color on purpose and cool the rest.
   - **Kind:** taste, argued from Itten. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- The white gutters between tiles mean no two strong hues touch, so no edge vibrates despite the loud palette.
- Every tile has a text label, so nothing depends on telling one color from another. The piece stays fine for viewers with color-vision deficiency.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The plain fields with centered pale circles look like placeholder art, either a picture that hasn't loaded or a stand-in. Check the live page: if real photographs replace them, findings 1 and 2 mostly go away and color moves to the photos.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 6 yes, 3 no (small palette; strong color kept to a small share; warm forward, cool recede)

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There are six picture tiles in a 3×2 grid.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No. All six tiles are flat colour fields with a paler disc at bottom centre, and none shows a picture: the tiles span x 60–437, 451–829 and 843–1220, at y 78–278 and 392–592. The captions under them name specific scenes, like "Climbing roses over the east gate", "Reeds and water lilies" and "Tomatoes in late July". The viewer of a "Garden show gallery" comes to see those gardens and gets six coloured swatches. The page's whole job, showing the show, isn't done. Every picture has the same disc layout and each tile just has its own hue, so they look like generated placeholders, not a chosen illustration style. They also tell the viewer nothing about how one garden differs from another. If the real photos failed to load, or this is a mock-up waiting for assets, the fix is to put in the actual photos of each scene. If this is meant as the final art, it needs real pictures or illustrations of each subject. Defect, judged as common sense (the catalog has no entry for this). Weight: major.
2. **Does each crop look intended, with no limb cut at a joint and no edges that just touch?** No. In every tile the bottom of the disc sits exactly on the tile's bottom edge, at y ≈ 278 on the top row and y ≈ 592 on the bottom row. When two edges just touch like this, the disc looks pinned to the frame or slightly off position. It looks neither placed inside the tile nor clearly cut by it. Fix: either lift the disc clear of the edge or crop it boldly so the cut is obviously intended. This only matters if the disc motif survives once there are real pictures. Taste (the catalog's sources aren't on the approved list). Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The six tiles share one rendering style, one size and one 2:1 shape, so the grid reads as a set and nothing jumps out. This is worth keeping once there are real photos: give them the same crop ratio and a matching colour treatment.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 10 yes, 2 no (every image shows its content; crops intended, no tangents), 0 unsure

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The image is a 3×2 gallery of six colour tiles, each with a pale circle (they look like image placeholders), plus a title and a caption under each tile. It has no chart, no table of figures and no dashboard.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: skipped. There are no visible controls: no buttons, links, fields, menus, navigation or messages. The page is a heading over a 3×2 grid of picture cards, each with a title and a one-line caption.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I can't tell whether the six cards (each colour tile at about 377×200 px plus its title and caption, such as "Rose arch" at x 60–437, y 78–330) are meant to be clicked. If they are, nothing about them says so at rest. There's no link styling, chevron, border or "View" cue, and the titles look like plain bold text. Check in a live browser whether the cards are links and whether hovering or focusing one changes anything. If they are clickable, they fail "Does every control look like what it does…", and keyboard focus visibility needs checking too.

**Checklist.** Interface: skipped
